title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(k\ge 3\) such that no deterministic algorithm decides k-SAT on n variables and input length L in time $O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}L^c)$ for any fixed constant c? Here k is fixed independently of n and L. This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis \((\mathrm{SETH})\).
definitions: A k-SAT input is an explicitly encoded conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most k literals \(x_{i}\) or \(\neg x_{i}\). Variables are relabeled consecutively and n counts the distinct variables actually present; L counts the full binary formula encoding, including literal indices and delimiters. The decision is exact satisfiability, with no promise about clause density, the number of satisfying assignments, or how the formula was generated. Empty clauses make the input unsatisfiable, and the empty conjunction is satisfiable. Running time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine time. For a fixed k, the algorithm, polynomial exponent, and hidden constant may depend on k and \(\varepsilon\), but not on the individual formula. Define \(s_{k}=\inf\){\(\alpha \ge 0 : k-\mathrm{SAT}\) has an \(O(2^{\alpha n}\mathrm{L}^{c})\)-time deterministic algorithm for some constant c}. SETH equivalently asserts \(\lim _{k}\to \infty s_{k}=1\); monotonicity follows because k-SAT is a restriction of \((k+1)-\mathrm{SAT}\). Polynomial factors are retained explicitly so reading the input is allowed even when clauses are repeated. No advice, oracle, random bits, or quantum computation is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

importance.reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates for k-SAT and their growth with clause width, using critical clauses and sparsification.
SETH-based reductions extend to numerous problems in polynomial time. Vassilevska Williams surveys the reductions, hypotheses, and resulting equivalence and hardness questions.
The parameterized-algorithms textbook gives explicit deterministic definitions of ETH and SETH and separately discusses their randomized analogues.

Jiang and Cai report randomized \(O*(1.307031578^{n})\) time for general 3-SAT and \(O*(1.306969598^{n})\) for Unique-3-SAT by refining the analysis of PPSZ. These are preprint bounds for fixed width, not a constant saving valid for every k.

status_note: The cited primary sources state SETH as an open hypothesis. Research through 10 September 2026 found no deterministic all-width constant-saving refutation or unrestricted proof. Bounds for a fixed width, random instances, restricted solvers, or unique satisfiability are not recorded as resolutions.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Recent work continues to sharpen small-width algorithms. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports a slightly improved randomized PPSZ bound for general 3-SAT, distinguished from its better bound under a unique-solution promise. Both the fixed width and use of randomness keep this improvement outside the deterministic, all-width saving required to refute the present statement.

sentences: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis concerns exact satisfiability of Boolean formulas with bounded clause width.
It asserts that no fixed positive saving over exhaustive search's exponent works for every fixed width.
Faster algorithms for small widths remain compatible with the hypothesis because their savings may vanish as width grows.
The statement underlies precise conditional running-time barriers for many polynomial-time problems.
The saved review fixes deterministic algorithms and emphasizes that neither a randomized improvement for 3-SAT nor ordinary \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) settles these stronger all-width quantifiers.
